TITLE: The Wobbly Table

(Sound of a table wobbling, then being adjusted)
Ever sat at a table that just… wouldn’t stay still? That’s where we’re starting today.

Welcome to Talk Therapy, the podcast about the small shifts that make a big difference. I’m your host, Sarah Miller, and I’m a firm believer that we often spend so much energy trying to *fix* things, we forget to simply *adjust* to them. We get caught up in grand gestures and overlook the power of the tiny tweaks. Today, we’re going to talk about that – about accepting a little wobble in life, and how adjusting *with* it can be more helpful than trying to eliminate it altogether.

I was at a friend’s house last week, helping her prep for a party. She’d gotten a beautiful, rustic farmhouse table, the kind you see in magazines. But one leg was just…off. She was frantic. She tried folding paper under it, wedging coasters, even attempting to shimmy the whole thing across the floor. Nothing worked. She was so focused on making it *perfect*, on having a stable surface for her guests, that she was getting increasingly stressed and actually delaying getting everything else done. Finally, I just said, “Okay, let’s just…work around it.” We put heavier items on the side with the short leg, and consciously placed things so the wobble wasn’t noticeable when people were setting down drinks. It wasn’t perfect, but it was *functional*, and honestly, no one even noticed. It made me think about how often we do that in our own lives.

We’re often taught to strive for stability, for control. To “fix” things, to make them “right.” And there’s value in that, of course. But life isn’t a perfectly level surface. There will always be wobbles – unexpected changes, challenging emotions, imperfect relationships. Trying to force everything into perfect alignment can be exhausting, and often impossible. It can lead to frustration, disappointment, and even a sense of failure when things inevitably…wobble.

What happens when we shift our focus from *eliminating* the wobble to *adjusting* to it? It’s about acknowledging that imperfection is part of the process. It’s about recognizing that sometimes, the most resourceful thing we can do isn't to fight against reality, but to work *with* it. Think of it like this: a rigid tree snaps in a strong wind. A flexible reed bends and survives. We aren’t reeds, but the principle holds true. Rigidity in our expectations or our approach can leave us broken when life throws something unexpected our way.

This isn’t about lowering our standards or accepting things we fundamentally disagree with. It's about recognizing what we can control and what we can't. We can't control the wobble, but we *can* control how we respond to it. We can choose to focus on what *is* working, on what we *can* do, even amidst the instability.

Let’s try a small exercise. Think of one thing in your life right now that feels…wobbly. Maybe it's a project at work that’s constantly changing direction, a relationship that feels uncertain, or even just your energy levels fluctuating throughout the day. Don't pick something huge or overwhelming; keep it relatively contained.

Now, instead of thinking about how to “fix” it, ask yourself these three questions: 1) What is one small adjustment I can make to work *with* this wobble? It could be as simple as shifting your schedule to accommodate lower energy levels, or asking for clarification on a project instead of trying to predict where it's going. 2) What resources do I already have that can help me navigate this? Think about your skills, your support system, even just your past experiences. 3) What would it look like to accept this wobble as temporary? To acknowledge that it doesn't define the whole picture?

Take just a minute now to quietly consider those questions for your chosen wobble. You don’t need to solve anything right now; just allow yourself to explore the possibility of adjustment instead of resistance. Notice any shift in your feelings as you reframe the situation. This isn't about pretending everything is okay; it's about finding a more sustainable way to navigate the uncertainty.

Sometimes, life isn’t about finding a perfectly stable table. It's about learning to balance your drink anyway. Thanks for listening to Talk Therapy. Remember, small shifts can make a big difference. Until next time, be kind to yourself and embrace the wobble.
